Big picture. Classical DIP makes image structure explicit (edges, regions, masks, geometry). CNNs learn local filters. Vision 
Transformers turn patches into tokens and learn relationships among them. These are complementary levels of representation,

Labs 7-10 | Filtering -> Segmentation -> Morphology -> Vision Transformer
1. From Image Classification to Pixel-Level Understanding
The word “segmentation” is often used loosely. For technically correct interpretation, distinguish the output required by the task:
Task What is predicted? Spatial output Separates same-class 
instances? Example
Image classification One or more labels for the whole 
image
No explicit location No “This image contains a cat.”
Object detection Class + bounding box for each 
object
Boxes Yes two cars -> two boxes
Semantic segmentation Class label for every pixel Dense class map No all road pixels share “road”
Instance segmentation Class + separate pixel mask for 
each instance
Dense instance masks Yes person #1, person #2
Panoptic segmentation Semantic map + instance 
identities for countable objects
Dense unified map Yes for “things” road + sky + separate cars
Terminology clarification. If “instant identification” is intended to mean identifying individual object instances, the standard 
terms are instance identification / instance segmentation. In the classical Lab 9 pipeline, connected-component labelling gives 
each disconnected foreground component an identity, but it does not by itself assign a semantic class.
1.1 Image classification
Image classification maps an input image x to a class label or class-probability vector. In a learned classifier, the model extracts 
features and then estimates p(class | image). The spatial extent of the object is not part of the required output.
• Classical rule-based classification: manually choose features such as area, perimeter, circularity, corners or texture, then 
apply explicit rules.
• KNN classification: store labelled feature vectors and classify a new vector from nearby training samples.
• CNN classification: learn convolution filters and hierarchical features jointly from labelled training data.
• ViT classification: use patch tokens and Transformer blocks; a classification head can use the [CLS] representation or pooled 
token features.
1.2 Segmentation
Segmentation partitions an image into meaningful pixel groups. Classical methods may group pixels by intensity, colour, 
connectivity or geometry; learned semantic/instance segmentation predicts pixel labels from data. A segmentation mask may be 
binary (foreground/background) or multi-class.

Critical distinction. A cluster is not automatically an object, and an edge map is not automatically a segmentation. K-means 
can assign the same cluster label to spatially disconnected regions; edge detection only highlights intensity transitions. Object 
identity requires additional spatial/semantic reasoning.
2. Lab 7 - Spatial Filtering, Gradients and Edge Evidence
Lab 7 provides the local-neighbourhood foundation for later segmentation. Smoothing reduces unwanted variation; derivative/high￾pass operators emphasize transitions that may correspond to boundaries.

% Sobel gradient and edge strength/direction
Sx = [-1 0 1; -2 0 2; -1 0 1];
Sy = [-1 -2 -1; 0 0 0; 1 2 1];
Gx = imfilter(I,Sx);

Technical clarification for MATLAB. The Lab 7 material describes neighbourhood filtering as convolution, but MATLAB 
imfilter(I,K) performs correlation by default. To request mathematical convolution explicitly, use imfilter(I,K,'conv'). For symmetric 
kernels (mean, Gaussian, many Laplacians) the result is the same; for asymmetric derivative kernels, sign/orientation can differ. 
Deep-learning libraries also commonly implement cross-correlation while calling the layer 'convolution'.

Previously generated course visual: fixed classical edge kernels versus learned CNN feature maps.
2.1 Canny edge detector: why it is more than “Sobel + threshold”
1. Gaussian smoothing reduces noise before differentiation.
2. Gradient components give magnitude and direction.
3. Non-maximum suppression keeps only local maxima along the gradient direction, producing thin candidates.
4. Double threshold separates strong, weak and rejected edge pixels.
5. Hysteresis keeps weak pixels that are connected to strong edges and rejects isolated weak responses.
Segmentation connection. Edges provide boundary evidence. A complete object mask usually needs region information, 
connectivity, contour closure, thresholding, morphology or a learned segmentation model.

3. Classical Image/Object Segmentation - Lab 8
3.1 Threshold-based segmentation
A binary threshold produces a mask BW(x,y). For a bright-object convention:
BW(x,y) = 1 if I(x,y) > T, otherwise 0.
Method Threshold definition Best situation Weakness
Manual global one user-chosen T for entire image stable illumination; known intensity 
separation
sensitive to lighting / subjective T
Otsu one data-driven global T roughly bimodal foreground/background 
histogram
fails when classes strongly overlap or 
illumination varies
Adaptive/local T(x,y) varies with neighbourhood uneven illumination / shadows window/sensitivity choices can create local 
noise
Otsu chooses a threshold that maximizes between-class variance (equivalently minimizes weighted within-class variance for the 
two classes). Adaptive thresholding estimates a local threshold surface rather than a single scalar.
3.2 K-means image segmentation
K-means is unsupervised clustering. Each pixel (or pixel feature vector) is assigned to the nearest cluster centroid. In Lab 8,
MATLAB imsegkmeans groups image pixels into K colour/intensity clusters and label2rgb visualizes the label matrix.
Objective: minimize sum of squared distances from samples to their assigned centroids: J = sum_k sum_{x in C_k} ||x -
mu_k||^2.
Do not over-interpret labels. K-means label 1/2/3... is an arbitrary cluster identity, not a semantic name. One cluster can 
appear in disconnected places; increasing K can split one real object into several colour clusters.
L = imsegkmeans(RGB,5);
M = label2rgb(L);
imshow(M);
% L is the numerical cluster-label matrix; M is only an RGB visualization.
3.3 Seed-based region growing: grayconnected
Region growing starts from a seed and accepts spatially connected pixels whose gray value is sufficiently similar to the seed value. 
The result is a logical binary mask.
[x,y] = ginput(1);
BW = grayconnected(Gray, round(y), round(x), 20);
imshow(BW);
• Why round? ginput returns continuous screen coordinates; array row/column indices must be integers.
• Why y before x? images use matrix indexing Gray(row,column), while ginput returns x=column and y=row.

4. Morphological Operators - Shape Processing of Binary Masks
Course-generated morphology summary used in Lab 9; detailed definitions and caveats follow below.
Morphology operates on object geometry using a structuring element (SE). For a binary foreground set A and structuring element 
B, the SE is translated across the image. The output depends on both SE shape and size.

4.1 Structuring element (SE)
• Square SE: isotropic for grid-aligned block-like neighbourhoods; larger size causes stronger erosion/dilation.
• Disk SE: approximately isotropic around the center; useful for rounded structures.
• Line SE: orientation-selective; useful for preserving/connecting line-like structures in a chosen direction.
• MATLAB Neighborhood property: the logical matrix showing which offsets belong to the SE.
SE3 = strel('square',3);
SEDisk = strel('disk',3,0); % radius 3, exact/no decomposition
SELine = strel('line',7,0); % length 7, angle 0 deg (horizontal)
imshow(SE3.Neighborhood);
4.2 Why erosion can be understood as a sliding logical test
For a flat 3x3 all-ones SE, move the SE center to each candidate foreground pixel. The output center is 1 only if every required SE 
position lies on foreground. If any required covered location is 0, that center becomes 0. This resembles sliding-window filtering 
geometrically, but it is not linear convolution: the operation is a set/min-type condition, not a weighted sum.
Grayscale morphology. For a flat structuring element, grayscale erosion behaves like a local minimum and grayscale dilation 
like a local maximum over the SE support. Binary morphology is the special case of set membership / 0-1 images.

5. Connectivity, Connected Components and Region Labelling - Lab 9
Neighbourhood Included neighbours Effect on diagonal contact
4-connectivity up, down, left, right diagonal-only pixels remain separate
8-connectivity 4-neighbours + four diagonals diagonal-only pixels can belong to same component
If two foreground pixels touch only at a corner, they are separate under 4-connectivity but connected under 8-connectivity. 
Connectivity is a definition of neighbourhood; it does not enhance the image.
[L4,N4] = bwlabel(BW,4);
[L8,N8] = bwlabel(BW,8);
CC4 = bwconncomp(BW,4);
CC8 = bwconncomp(BW,8);
Labelling rule. The numeric labels produced by bwlabel identify connected components according to scan/labelling order, not 
object size. If you want the largest object to be label 1, sort components by area and relabel explicitly.
5.1 From mask to object measurements
stats = regionprops(L,'Area','Centroid','BoundingBox','Perimeter');
Property Meaning Use
Area number of foreground pixels in region size filtering; object comparison
Centroid geometric center in image coordinates tracking / annotation / location
BoundingBox axis-aligned rectangle enclosing region object localization / crop
Perimeter estimated boundary length shape descriptors / compactness
A common classical pipeline for coins/pills/bolts/cells is: grayscale -> threshold -> morphology -> remove small components -> 
connected components -> label -> regionprops -> count/measure/extract.

6.1 Losses and evaluation
For multi-class semantic segmentation, a common training loss is pixel-wise cross-entropy. For foreground/background masks, 
binary cross-entropy and Dice-style losses are common. Evaluation should not rely only on pixel accuracy when class imbalance is 
strong.
Metric Formula / idea Interpretation
IoU / Jaccard TP / (TP + FP + FN) overlap of predicted and true region
Dice / F1 mask 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) overlap with stronger weighting of intersection
Pixel accuracy correct pixels / all pixels can be misleading if background dominates
Mean IoU average IoU across classes standard semantic segmentation summary
Detection AP precision-recall across IoU thresholds object detection / instance segmentation evaluation
6.2 Classical-to-modern connection
• Thresholding -> learned logits: classical T is hand-chosen; a network learns a decision function from data.
• Morphology -> post-processing: opening/closing/connected components can still clean learned masks when application 
constraints justify it.
• regionprops -> object analytics: even after a neural mask, area, perimeter, centroid and shape statistics remain useful.
• Edges -> boundary-aware learning: gradient/boundary cues can be auxiliary losses/features in segmentation systems.

8. Transformer Mechanism - What Attention Actually Computes
Let X be a sequence of token representations. A self-attention head computes learned linear projections:
Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
• Query (Q): what the current token is looking for in the context.
• Key (K): what each token offers for matching.
• Value (V): the information mixed after attention weights are computed.
• Attention matrix: row i contains the probability-like weights from query token i to all key tokens after softmax.
• Multi-head attention: several Q/K/V projections run in parallel, allowing different relation patterns; their outputs are 
concatenated/projected.
• Transformer block: attention sublayer + residual/norm + feed-forward/MLP sublayer + residual/norm (exact pre-norm/post￾norm ordering depends on architecture).
Attention is not “meaning” by itself. Semantic knowledge is distributed across learned embeddings, attention/MLP weights 
and representations produced by many layers. A high attention value is an association used by that head/layer; it is not proof of 
causality, visual similarity or a named concept.

9. Vision Transformer (ViT) - Lab 10 in Detail
The supplied Lab 10 notebook uses a pretrained ViT base model with 224x224 input and 16x16 patches. Therefore 14x14 = 196 
image patches are formed. A special [CLS] token makes 197 tokens. The notebook analyses real returned attention tensors and 
contextual patch features.
Quantity Lab 10 value / meaning
Input image 224 x 224 RGB
Patch size 16 x 16
Spatial patch grid 14 x 14
Image patch tokens 196
Special token [CLS] = token 0 in the teaching notebook
Total tokens 197
ViT-base blocks 12 Transformer encoder blocks
Attention heads 12 per block
Attention matrix per head 197 x 197
Hidden embedding size 768 for ViT-Base
Per-head key/query dimension 768 / 12 = 64 (for standard ViT-Base configuration)
Patch vector vs embedding. A 16x16 RGB patch contains 16x16x3 = 768 raw numbers, but ViT still applies a learned patch￾projection layer. The equality between raw patch dimension 768 and ViT-Base hidden size 768 is specific to this common 
configuration, not a general rule for all ViTs.

9.1 Positional information and [CLS]
Attention by itself is permutation-equivariant: it does not know that one patch is “top-left” and another is “bottom-right.” ViT adds 
learned positional embeddings (or another positional scheme) so spatial location is represented. The [CLS] token is a learned
token intended to accumulate a global representation for tasks such as classification; it is not an image patch.
9.2 Layer and head interpretation
• Head: one parallel attention projection inside a block. Different heads can focus on different relationships.
• Layer/block: a sequential transformation stage. Layer 6 receives the representation produced by layers 1-5 and produces 
layer-6 features.
• Selecting layer 6 in the notebook: this selects the stored layer-6 attention for analysis; the normal forward pass still 
computes all 12 blocks unless the model is explicitly truncated or early-exited.
• Selecting a query patch: choose one row of the attention matrix; that row describes where that query token assigns attention 
across keys in that head/layer.
SELECT_LAYER = 12
SELECT_HEAD = 1
QUERY_TOKEN = 88
A = attentions[SELECT_LAYER-1][SELECT_HEAD-1] # 197 x 197
query_row = A[QUERY_TOKEN].copy()

similarity

Why Lab 10 is retrieval, not generation. The notebook uses an intact query patch to retrieve a similar patch from other 
photographs, then substitutes it. It does not infer truly missing pixels from surrounding context. MAE/inpainting/diffusion-style

10. GPT-Style Transformer vs ViT
GPT-style language models and ViT share the Transformer attention idea, but they use different tokenization and attention 
constraints. The key distinction is encoder-style bidirectional visual attention versus decoder-style causal language modeling.
Aspect ViT encoder GPT-style decoder-only Transformer
Token image patch embedding (+ [CLS] in many designs) text/subword token embedding
Position 2-D image position encoded into token sequence 1-D token order / positional representation
Self-attention normally bidirectional: each token can attend to all tokens causal: token t cannot attend to future tokens t+1...
Primary pretraining/task 
family
image representation/classification/self-supervised variants next-token prediction / autoregressive generation
Typical output image/patch representation; task head probability distribution over next token
Mask no causal mask in standard ViT encoder triangular causal mask
Relation to prompts not normally prompted with natural-language text by itself prompt tokens condition subsequent generation
10.1 Where does the “meaning” of dog or ball come from?
A Transformer is the architecture. An LLM is a Transformer-based model whose parameters are learned from large-scale language 
training. Token embeddings start as learned vectors and become contextualized through repeated attention and MLP 
transformations. Meaning-like statistical/semantic structure is therefore distributed through the learned parameters and activations; 
there is not a separate “LLM” sitting inside each Transformer block.
10.2 What is the role of a prompt?
A prompt is the current input context and instruction. Its tokens are processed by the model and condition the activations and 
probability distribution for subsequent outputs. A prompt normally does not permanently retrain the model; it changes the current 
computation. In a text-plus-document question-answering setting, the inserted text supplies temporary context and the question 
constrains what answer should be generated.
More precise than “the prompt directs attention.” Attention patterns can change because the prompt changes the token 
sequence and representations, but the prompt is not a manual switch that explicitly tells an attention head where to look. The 
learned network determines the attention weights from Q and K at inference time.
10.3 VLM connection
A Vision-Language Model connects visual representations with language. Common designs encode an image into visual 
tokens/features and align/project them into a language model or use cross-attention/unified multimodal tokens. This allows image 
captioning, visual question answering and multimodal reasoning. A plain GPT-style text model does not directly “see” pixels unless 
a vision pathway is added.

12.1 A “dashboard” mindset for a DIP project
A dashboard is useful only if it exposes meaningful visual and quantitative evidence. A strong DIP dashboard should not hide the 
processing behind one final label. It should show input, intermediate stages, parameters, output and metrics.

13. High-Value Technical Clarifications / Common Mistakes
Statement Correct interpretation
“K-means gives K objects.” No. It gives K clusters; each cluster can be spatially disconnected.
“Multiple grayconnected seeds give separate 
labels.”
Not if masks are OR-combined; the result is binary unless separate masks/labels are retained.
“Opening fills holes.” Not generally. Opening removes small foreground structures; closing can close small background gaps/holes; 
imfill fills enclosed holes.
“Erosion is convolution with a 3x3 ones 
mask.”
No. Erosion is a nonlinear/set-min operation; sliding-window geometry is similar but arithmetic is different.
“8-connectivity enhances diagonal edges.” No. It changes the definition of connectedness.
“Edge = object boundary.” An edge is local intensity change; object boundaries require grouping/segmentation.
“Semantic segmentation identifies each car 
separately.”
No. Same-class pixels share one class label; instance segmentation separates individual cars.
“Attention is similarity.” Not necessarily. Attention is task/context-dependent Q-K weighting; cosine similarity of hidden features is a 
different calculation.
“Selecting ViT layer 6 makes the model run 
only six layers.”
Not in the standard full forward pass used in Lab 10; layer selection is for analysis unless the model is 
explicitly truncated.
“GPT is inside a Transformer.” GPT is a model built from Transformer decoder blocks; the architecture is not a separate component inside 
an LLM.
“A prompt permanently teaches the model.” Normally no; the prompt conditions the current inference context unless a separate training/memory 
mechanism is used.
“Lab 10 reconstructs a missing patch.” No. It retrieves/substitutes a patch using features; true missing-patch prediction needs a 
generative/reconstruction model.
